title: Outdoor rabbit run flooring options
subtitle: Choosing a surface that is safe, hygienic, and easy to maintain.
excerpt: The floor of an outdoor rabbit run affects welfare, hygiene, and ease of management in roughly equal measure. Bare earth lets rabbits dig and graze, which is good for enrichment, but concentrates disease risk and can allow escape. Hard or covered surfaces are easier to clean but deprive rabbits of natural behaviour. Most keepers use a combination.
sourceNotes: RSPCA, Welfare Needs of Rabbits (2023). British Rabbit Council, Accommodation Standards (2022). Rabbit Welfare Association and Fund, Housing Guidance (2021).

glossaryTerms.definition: A welded wire or weld mesh floor used in rabbit housing. Allows droppings to fall through but risks sore hocks and is now disfavoured in UK welfare guidance.

content.text: Rabbit run flooring is a practical choice that most keepers revisit several times as they learn what works on their land. There is no single right answer, but each surface type has predictable strengths and weaknesses.

Grass and earth are the most natural surface and allow digging, foraging, and grazing. The main problems are disease build-up (coccidiosis, E. cuniculi oocysts, and worm larvae survive in soil for months), escape by digging, and rapid poaching in wet conditions. On a wet UK winter lawn, a permanent earth run quickly becomes a mud pit.
Rotate the run's position every 4 to 6 weeks if the run is lightweight and movable.
Sink a skirt of wire mesh 30 to 40 cm into the ground around the perimeter to prevent digging out.

Hard surfaces are very easy to clean and disinfect, and eliminate the disease risk from contaminated soil. The welfare drawback is that concrete does not allow any digging or foraging. Provide a deep tray of loose soil or a dig box filled with child-safe play sand as an enrichment substitute. Hard floors also wear hock fur; supply deep hay bedding to give the rabbit somewhere soft to rest.

Both surfaces drain well, reduce mud, and provide some cushioning. Pea gravel cleans easily with a hose; bark chip retains moisture and needs replacing regularly. Neither surface is suitable as the sole substrate: provide hay bedding and a grass section alongside wherever possible.

They can cause sore hocks, particularly in Rex breeds with thin foot fur. If you inherit hutches with wire floors, cover them with a solid panel or deep layer of hay.
Sleeping area and hutch: solid wood floor with thick hay bedding, changed twice weekly.
Run attached to hutch: pea gravel or concrete with a hay-filled corner and a dig box.
Exercise time: supervised grass time on a rotation, ideally daily in fine weather.

attrs.cue: Run floor becomes permanently wet and muddy in autumn
attrs.cause: Drainage blocked or naturally poor-draining clay soil
attrs.fix: Add a 10 cm layer of sharp sand beneath pea gravel to improve drainage. In the worst areas, lay a woven landscape fabric under the gravel to prevent it sinking into the clay.

attrs.cue: Rabbits developing sore hocks (bald, inflamed patches on the underside of the feet)
attrs.cause: Hard floor without adequate bedding, or wire mesh floor
attrs.fix: Ensure deep hay bedding is always available as a resting area. Cover any wire floors immediately. A rabbit with sore hocks needs veterinary attention as infections can penetrate the bone.
